sysd-scale-015.title: Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors
sysd-scale-015.text:
Google's Chubby lock service and Megastore run on Paxos, and so do the leader elections of DynamoDB. Paxos is a family of protocols for solving consensus in a network of unreliable or fallible processors. It is usually used where durability is required, such as replicating a file or a database whose durable state may be large. In most deployments each process plays three roles: Proposer, Acceptor and Learner. Merging the roles collapses the protocol into an efficient client-master-replica style deployment.

Safety is always guaranteed: only proposed values can be chosen (validity), and no two learners can learn different values (agreement), whatever the pattern of failures. Termination is not guaranteed. That is consistent with the FLP result that no protocol can have safety, liveness and failure tolerance all at once. The conditions that stall progress are difficult to provoke. A group can make progress with n = 2F + 1 processors despite F simultaneous failures, because the non-faulty processes must outnumber the faulty ones. It also runs inside the database described in {{ref:sysd-scale-026}}, while Cassandra uses it only for lightweight transactions.

sysd-scale-109.title: Byzantine fault tolerance: agreeing when some nodes lie
sysd-scale-109.text:
In the Byzantine generals allegory, the generals must agree on one plan, but traitors may vote selectively, telling some to attack and others to retreat. A Byzantine fault is a fault that presents different symptoms to different observers, including imperfect information on whether a component has failed. Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is resilience to such conditions. A fail-stop failure is only a crash that other nodes detect. A Byzantine node can emit arbitrary data, even looking healthy to some nodes, so it is the hardest failure class.

Tolerating F Byzantine failures needs at least 3F+1 participants, 2F+1 independent communication paths and F+1 rounds of communication. Majority-quorum consensus that tolerates only crashes needs just 2f+1 replicas for f failures. With unforgeable digital signatures, one commander and two lieutenants can reach consensus despite a single traitor, who cannot impersonate others. BFT guarantees only that components receive the same value; it does not check the value. Blockchains use BFT-based consensus such as PBFT, Tendermint and Avalanche, and Boeing 777 flight control uses BFT too.

sysd-scale-021.title: Raft: consensus built to be understood
sysd-scale-021.text:
Raft was designed with an aim that is rare in this field: to be understandable. It is a consensus algorithm created as an alternative to the Paxos family, with its logic separated into parts, yet formally proven safe. It distributes a state machine across a cluster so that every node agrees on the same series of state transitions.

Raft reaches agreement through one elected leader, which alone manages log replication and decides where new entries go without consulting the other servers. Each server is a leader or a follower, or a candidate during an election. Among its guarantees is election safety: one leader per term. In its base form Raft does not tolerate Byzantine failures: nodes trust the elected leader and assume all participants are trustworthy. The single-leader model also sends all reads, writes and log replication through one leader, a single point of failure and a bottleneck. Raft keeps the replicated log of the store described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-052}}, CockroachDB uses it in its replication layer, and MongoDB uses a variant in its replica sets.

sysd-scale-115.title: Consensus-based system patterns: where agreement gets used
sysd-scale-115.text:
Almost nobody runs a consensus algorithm bare. These algorithms only let nodes agree on a value once, so they live inside higher-level components such as datastores, configuration stores, queues, locks and leader election services. Using such components reduces complexity for designers and lets the underlying algorithm change. Many systems use consensus as clients of a service such as ZooKeeper, Google's Chubby or the one in {{ref:sysd-msg-144}}.

Each pattern has its own cost. Replicated datastores apply replicated state machines and put consensus in the critical path, so performance, throughput and scale matter, and the read consistency on offer greatly affects scaling. A single leader gives coarse-grained mutual exclusion. A service written as a simple program can be made highly available by replicating it and electing one leader, which takes consensus off the critical path. A barrier blocks a group of processes until a condition is met, splitting a computation into phases. A large data-processing job, covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-040}}, uses one when it waits for its whole Map phase. A lone coordinator would be a single point of failure, so use a replicated state machine. Distributed queues should use leases rather than outright removal, so claimed tasks are processed. Queues and publish-subscribe systems often need good throughput but not very low latency, and atomic broadcast suits them well.

sysd-scale-117.title: Sizing a consensus group: why five replicas are common
sysd-scale-117.text:
Adding a sixth replica can make a group less available than it was with five. Consensus systems use majority quorums, so a group of 2f + 1 replicas tolerates f failures. The number of replicas is one of the most critical deployment decisions. Without Byzantine tolerance the minimum is three replicas, which tolerate one failure; with two, no failure can be tolerated. Byzantine tolerance needs 3f + 1 replicas for f failures.

Most downtime is planned maintenance, which three replicas survive, but an unplanned failure during maintenance makes the group unavailable. Five replicas are therefore recommended, tolerating two failures. A typical ZooKeeper or Chubby deployment uses five replicas, needs three for quorum and survives two (40%) down. With six, four are needed and only 33% can be down. Each replica costs resources, and where every shard is a full consensus group the cost grows with the shard count. The number of replicas trades off reliability, frequency of planned maintenance and performance.

sysd-scale-118.title: Placing consensus replicas across failure domains
sysd-scale-118.text:
Keep every replica in one rack and a single rack failure ends the service. Spread them across the world and every write waits on a long round trip. Where to put a consensus group's processes trades off the failure domains the system should survive against its latency requirements. A failure domain is the set of components one failure can make unavailable, such as a machine, a rack, a datacenter or a region.

As replicas move farther apart they survive bigger failures, but round-trip time and operation latency rise. If all clients sit in one domain, spreading further adds cost and latency for no benefit. Client-perceived latency is the key measure, so place replicas to minimize client round-trip time. Colocating replicas can hurt availability: with five datacenters and a sixth replica added in one, an outage there removes both spare replicas and cuts capacity by 33%. Sending every read to the nearest replica can cascade, as a load spike overwhelms it, then the next closest, and so on.

sysd-scale-016.title: Basic Paxos: prepare, promise, accept, accepted
sysd-scale-016.text:
Basic Paxos decides a single value in two phases, and each phase has two messages. It is the simplest Paxos protocol: each instance decides one output value over one or more rounds. In phase 1a, Prepare, a Proposer sends a Prepare message to at least a quorum of Acceptors, carrying a unique number n greater than any it used before. The number only identifies the message; it is not the proposed value. In phase 1b, Promise, an Acceptor that sees an n higher than any before replies with a promise. It will ignore proposals numbered n or lower, and it reports the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted, with its value.

Once a quorum has promised, phase 2a, Accept, begins. The Proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported, or its own value if none was reported. In phase 2b, Accepted, an Acceptor accepts (n, v) unless it has promised to consider only higher-numbered proposals, then tells the Proposer and the Learners. Learners learn the value after Accepted messages from a majority of Acceptors.

Consensus is reached when a majority of Acceptors accept the same identifier number. Because each identifier carries one value, they accept the same value, and the chosen value is permanent and immutable. A round fails when Proposers send conflicting Prepares or no quorum answers, and a new round starts with a higher number. Losing one Acceptor while a quorum remains, or a redundant Learner, needs no recovery.

sysd-scale-017.title: Multi-Paxos: skipping the first phase with a stable leader
sysd-scale-017.text: A replicated state machine needs a continuous stream of agreed commands, and running a full Basic Paxos for each one would add a significant amount of overhead. Multi-Paxos runs a continuous series of Basic Paxos instances, with a stable leader, to agree on that stream. Clients send commands to the leader, which assigns each a new command number i and starts the ith instance of the algorithm with the acceptors. If the leader is stable, phase 1 (Prepare and Promise) can be skipped for later instances with the same leader. The round number I travels with each value. That cuts the failure-free message delay from proposal to learning from 4 delays to 2. A common deployment collapses Proposer, Acceptor and Learner into one Server role, leaving just Clients and Servers.

sysd-scale-013.title: Permissioned and permissionless consensus
sysd-scale-013.text: If anyone can join a group, one attacker can pretend to be many members. Permissioned consensus runs among a fixed, known group of authenticated participants, while permissionless consensus lets anyone join dynamically. Without a closed group, a Sybil attack can defeat even a Byzantine-tolerant algorithm by creating enough virtual participants to overwhelm its threshold. Permissionless protocols counter it with an artificial cost of entry. Bitcoin's proof of work has participants compete to solve hash puzzles, earning the right to commit blocks in proportion to computational effort. Because proof of work is energy-hungry, later protocols use proof of stake, proof of space or proof of authority instead.

sysd-scale-119.title: Monitoring consensus systems: what to watch
sysd-scale-119.text: A consensus group can look healthy while making no progress. Operators track how many members each group has and each one's status. A process may run yet be unable to progress, lag persistently, recover state from peers, be up to date, or lead. A leader-based system such as Multi-Paxos with no leader is totally unavailable, so the existence of a leader must be watched. Rapid leadership changes hurt performance. A term or view number marks each change: a fast increase signals a flapping leader, perhaps from network problems, and a decrease signals a serious bug. In a healthy system the consensus transaction number keeps rising.

sysd-scale-019.title: Cheap Paxos: tolerating failures with cheap spare machines
sysd-scale-019.text: Some machines in a consensus group can be cheap. Cheap Paxos extends Basic Paxos to tolerate F failures with F + 1 main processors and F auxiliary processors, by dynamically reconfiguring after each failure. In stable periods the auxiliary processors take no part in the protocol, so they can be small, slow or cheap, or mainly devoted to other tasks. The saving costs liveness: if too many main processors fail in a short time, the system must halt until the auxiliary processors can reconfigure it. A third processor is needed because with only two, one cannot tell the failure of the other from failure of the communication medium.

sysd-scale-018.title: Fast Paxos: trading replicas for fewer message delays
sysd-scale-018.text: Fast Paxos generalizes Basic Paxos to reduce end-to-end message delays. Basic Paxos takes 3 message delays from client request to learning; Fast Paxos allows 2. The price is more machines and more work for the client. It needs 3f + 1 acceptors to tolerate f faults, against 2f + 1 classically, and the client must send its request to multiple destinations. When proposals collide, recovery by the leader with a new round takes four message delays. If the leader specifies a recovery technique in advance, acceptors recover themselves in three delays, or two if all Learners are also Acceptors.

sysd-scale-116.title: Consensus performance: round trips and disk writes
sysd-scale-116.text:
Consensus has a reputation for being too slow for high throughput and low latency. The Google SRE book says this is untrue: implementations can be slow, but a number of techniques improve performance. Performance depends on the workload and on the deployment. Two physical limits matter most: network round-trip time and the time to write to persistent storage. Round trips take about a millisecond within a datacenter, a typical 45 milliseconds within the United States and 70 from New York to London.

Acceptors must log commitments to disk so a restarted node honors them. A write takes one to several milliseconds, and if a small random write takes about 10 milliseconds, consensus is limited to roughly 100 operations per second. Batching several client operations into one proposal amortizes the fixed costs of disk logging and network latency. Pipelining keeps several proposals in flight without breaking global ordering. Stable-leader protocols, such as the one in {{ref:sysd-scale-017}}, need only one round trip to a quorum, but every write goes through the leader, so distant clients pay latency.

sysd-scale-022.title: Raft leader election: terms, timeouts and votes
sysd-scale-022.text: Silence is how Raft detects a dead leader. The leader sends heartbeat messages, and each follower has a timeout, typically 150 to 300 ms, for hearing one. A follower that hears nothing for the election timeout becomes a candidate. It increases the term counter, votes for itself and requests votes from all other servers. Each server votes once per term, first come first served, and a majority of votes makes the candidate leader. A candidate that sees a larger term number steps down to follower. On a split vote a new term and election start, and a randomized election timeout makes repeated split votes unlikely.

sysd-scale-023.title: Raft log replication: how followers catch up
sysd-scale-023.text: In Raft the leader accepts client requests, appends them to its log and replicates them to the followers. It forwards each new entry as an AppendEntries message and retries indefinitely if a follower is unavailable. Once half or more of the followers confirm, the entry is committed, and so are all earlier entries. After a leader crash, logs may be inconsistent. The new leader finds the last entry where a follower's log agrees with its own, deletes the follower's later entries and replaces them with its own. A candidate cannot win an election unless its log contains all committed entries.

sysd-scale-005.title: The saga pattern: local transactions with undo steps
sysd-scale-005.text:
Distributed transactions are hard to scale and can hurt performance, so the saga pattern gives up the single big commit. A saga is a sequence of local transactions that together do the work of one distributed transaction. Each local transaction updates its own database and then publishes a message or event that triggers the next one. If one fails, for example by violating a business rule, the saga runs undo steps that reverse the changes made by the earlier local transactions; see {{ref:sysd-scale-110}}.

Sagas keep data consistent across services that each own their database. There are two ways to coordinate one. In choreography, each local transaction publishes domain events that trigger local transactions in other services. In orchestration, an orchestrator tells the participants which local transactions to run. The 1987 paper proposed sagas because long-lived transactions hold database resources for a long time, which significantly delays the shorter and more common ones. The costs are real: sagas are hard to debug and test, risk cyclic dependencies between participants, and lack of participant data isolation causes durability challenges.

sysd-scale-110.title: Compensating transactions: undoing committed work
sysd-scale-110.text: Some mistakes cannot be rolled back. A compensating transaction is a transaction that reverses the effects of a previously committed transaction. It is needed when a business process fails after some steps have committed. Unlike a rollback, which discards uncommitted changes, it is a new transaction. It applies business logic to undo completed work, such as crediting $100 to undo a debit of $100. On failure, the compensations of completed steps run in reverse order. It is fundamental to the saga pattern. The limits: results are visible before they are compensated, a compensation can itself fail, and some effects, such as a sent email, cannot be undone.

openers.consensus-ordering-and-distributed-trans: A single database can promise that a transaction is all-or-nothing. Once the data lives on several machines, that promise has to be rebuilt from messages between them, and the machines can fail or disagree about the time. This chapter starts with the distributed transaction and the voting protocol that completes one. It then turns to how machines order events without a shared clock, how they notice that a peer has died, and how a group of them can agree on a single value even when some fail. That agreement problem is the foundation for distributed locks, leader election and replicated state machines.

reviews.consensus-ordering-and-distributed-trans: Every thread in this chapter starts from the same fact: machines fail and messages arrive late, so nobody can be sure what the others know. Two-phase commit and three-phase commit make several databases agree on a commit, while the saga pattern gives up the single commit and relies on local transactions and compensating transactions. Lamport timestamps and vector clocks order events without a shared clock, and heartbeats tell a cluster which members are still alive. Consensus lets a group agree on a value, or a series of them, through Paxos and Raft, and it underlies replicated state machines, distributed locks and ZooKeeper. Even consensus has limits: the FLP result, the Two Generals' Problem and Byzantine failures mark what no protocol can promise, and the size and placement of the group decide how well it works in practice.
